title: Learning syntax without semantics: Disentangled tiny language models
claim: Models trained on content-free grammatical text keep a strong syntax preference while showing no semantic-plausibility preference, unlike normally trained models.
layout: single scatter panel, two axes, dashed zero-reference lines, two colored clusters
description: A single scatter plot. The x-axis is the semantics margin ΔK, from about -1 to 17. The y-axis is the syntax margin ΔG, from about -13 to 15. Dashed blue lines mark x=0 and y=0 and divide the plot into quadrants. Blue points are the Normal LM. They spread widely: ΔK is mostly positive, between 1 and 16, and ΔG ranges from -13 to 14. Orange points are SAMBAL. They form a tight vertical column at ΔK≈0, with ΔG mostly positive, between 0 and 15. The legend sits at top right. The eye goes first to the orange column hugging the vertical dashed line, set against the broad blue cloud. This shows that syntax is separated from semantics.
caption: Syntax margin vs. semantic-plausibility margin on minimal sentence pairs. Models trained on grammatical nonsense (SAMBAL, orange) show a preference for syntactically-correct sentences, with positive logit margin ∆G = log P (grammatical) −log P (ungrammatical), but no preference for semantically-plausible sentences, with logit margin ∆K = log P (plausible) −log P (implausible) near zero, unlike a normally trained LM (§4.3).
abstract: Language models acquire syntax and world knowledge together, entangling the two in ways that limit efficiency and controllability. We show that syntax can be learned while suppressing semantic plausibility and world‑knowledge cues, yielding more efficient and controllable models. We train tiny LMs on grammatical nonsense — syntactically well-formed text with semantic content ablated via constrained relexicalization (SAMBAL). Models trained on this data perform comparably to standard pretraining on syntactic benchmarks (BLiMP, SyntaxGym) while scoring at chance on world knowledge probes (EWoK). On targeted grammar-plausibility conflict probes, content-neutral models prefer grammaticality where standard models prefer plausibility, and their representations show more syntactic vs lexical alignment. On efficiency, disentanglement yields substantial sample and parameter gains: in low‑resource regimes, a 5M‑parameter model matches a 30M‑parameter baseline at the same data budget. On controllability, content-neutral models adapt rapidly to a new domain with minimal exposure, suggesting the feasibility of modular post‑hoc knowledge specialization.
